lessons.title: Workplace exposure on processing lines
lessons.html:
Workplace exposure on processing lines

This workplace module requires sustained experience operating processing lines in a real mill, typically pelleting, cooling, crumbling and screening, and where available expansion, extrusion, post-pellet liquid application and bagging. At this level you are expected to run lines independently, optimise them and guide others.

Range of exposure

  • Several product types: for example broiler starter crumbles, broiler grower pellets, layer mash or pellets, dairy and beef pellets, and if available pet or aqua feeds.
  • Die changes and roller adjustments.
  • Start-up, steady running, changeovers and shutdowns.
  • Process deviations: chokes, high fines, steam problems, cooler overheating.
  • Hygiene critical control points, such as conditioning time and temperature for heat-treated feeds.
  • Post-pellet liquid application of fat or enzymes.
  • Bulk loading and bagging of finished feed.

Optimisation projects

A strong portfolio includes at least one improvement you were involved in, with data before and after. Examples:

  • Reducing fines on a product by adjusting conditioning within specification.
  • Raising throughput (t/h) by tuning feed rate and steam quality.
  • Reducing energy per tonne by cutting idle running.
  • Shortening die change time with better preparation.

Use the mill's data: process logs, PDI results, downtime logs and energy readings. Agree any change with your mentor and the process owner before trying it, and stay within the approved specification.

Evidence

EvidencePurpose
Process logs and quality results you producedShows routine competence
Mentor observation of start-up, changeover and shutdownShows correct procedure
Deviation and choke reportsShows problem-solving and safe practice
Improvement project summaryShows analysis and optimisation
Record of coaching a junior operatorShows guidance of others

lessons.title: Professional practice on the line
lessons.html:
Professional practice on the line

Running to specification

  • Know the process specification for each product: conditioning targets, die, PDI target, cooler outlet temperature and moisture.
  • Record readings at the set interval and act on trends.
  • Hold product that fails a critical limit; never 'fix' records.
  • Communicate with the mixer operator so mash supply matches line capacity and the sequence plan.

Problem-solving approach

  1. Observe and measure: what exactly is wrong, since when, on which product?
  2. Check the obvious: steam pressure and quality, mash condition, die and rollers, cooler settings.
  3. Change one variable at a time and record the result.
  4. Escalate when the fix is outside your authority or the specification.
  5. Record the cause and solution so others learn.

Safety leadership

  • Always lock out and verify zero energy before clearing chokes, opening doors or changing dies.
  • Use die-handling equipment.
  • Respect hot surfaces and steam; keep insulation in place.
  • Watch for smouldering in coolers and pellet mills; know the fire response.
  • Model these behaviours; junior operators copy what you do, not what you say.

Coaching others

Explain the reason behind each action. Let the junior operator perform the task while you observe, then give specific feedback. Check their records. Sign off only when they are consistently competent.

Communication and handover

At shift change, hand over line status, product in progress, die condition, open faults, quality holds and any changes to settings, verbally and in writing.

Key points

  • Gain experience across products, start-ups, changeovers and deviations.
  • Include a data-based improvement in your portfolio.
  • Change one variable at a time and stay within specification.
  • Lead safety by example: lockout, die handling, fire awareness.
  • Coach junior operators and hand over thoroughly.
